extracted.intended_audience: journalists, public affairs professionals, corporate communications staff
extracted.subtask_description: Creating a corporate press release announcing a new report or survey, summarizing key findings, providing contact info and organizational boilerplate, and directing readers to full reports and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline / Title
rubrics_metrics.description: New Report: Pressure for Corporate Engagement in Social Issues is Growing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concise, newsy headline that states the document type (e.g., 'New Report') and the principal takeaway. It should be attention-grabbing and accurately reflect the main finding without overclaiming. Avoid vague or purely promotional language; prefer clear, factual phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release marking and timing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly indicate the release status (e.g., 'FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE') and include the release date. This orients media and recipients to timing and embargo rules. Do not omit or mislabel the timing; if embargoed, state embargo terms explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact block (media contact information)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Contact:
Laura Horsley
Senior Director of Marketing and Communications
Public Affairs Council
[email protected]
| 202.787.5963
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a named contact with title, organization, email, and phone so reporters can follow up. Prefer a direct person and phone number; avoid only generic inboxes when possible. Ensure contact details are current and responsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline / location
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the lead paragraph with a dateline (city) followed by a dash to indicate the origin of the release. This provides geographic context and is standard press-release format. If multiple locations are relevant, choose the most newsworthy or organizationally relevant city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead paragraph summarizing the main point
rubrics_metrics.description: Major corporations are feeling increased pressure from stakeholders — especially employees — to take a stand on social issues, according to a new report from the Foundation for Public Affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a succinct lead that summarizes the core news (what, who, why/so-what). The lead should name the report/study and the principal finding. Avoid burying the key point deep in the body; the lead must answer why readers should care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report title and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Released today, Lobbying for Good explores why companies decide to embrace social issues and how they set priorities, determine key strategies and spokespeople, and measure results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly name the report and describe its scope/angle (e.g., survey + practical insights). Link the title to the report when possible. This orients readers to the source and focus of the findings; do not use shorthand or internal acronyms without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an authoritative quote
rubrics_metrics.description: “Public expectations have risen substantially for large corporations when it comes to addressing important social issues, but each company needs to determine its own path to engagement,” said Public Affairs Council President Doug Pinkham.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a short, attributable quote from an organizational leader to add interpretation and human voice. The quote should contextualize findings, convey the organization's stance, and be attributable (name and title). Avoid long, jargon-heavy quotes; keep them quotable and newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key findings / topline bullet list
rubrics_metrics.description:
Key findings include:
Pressure to engage is increasing. Nine out of 10 (91%) major companies believe pressure to engage in social issues has increased in the past three years... An even higher percentage of firms (96%) believe these expectations will rise further in the next three years... Companies are taking a stand on civil rights issues... Political action is the most common way companies engage... Forty percent (40%) of respondents updated their PAC contribution criteria...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the most newsworthy statistics and comparisons in a clear, bulleted 'Key findings' list. Use specific percentages and comparisons (e.g., vs. 2016) to show trends. Bullets should be concise, data-driven, and prioritized by news value. Avoid vague claims without numbers or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear description of strategies and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Political action is the most common way companies engage in social issues. Forty-three percent (43%) used internal or contract lobbyists... Similar to 2016, the most common strategy is joining a coalition. The second most common strategy is issuing a public statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing how subjects act, enumerate concrete strategies and give prevalence where available. Use examples (lobbying, coalitions, statements, PAC updates) to make abstract findings actionable. Avoid generic descriptors without examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of drivers and stakeholder breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders, rather than reputation or business needs, are driving issue engagement. Stakeholder demands were the most common reason... The two most influential groups of stakeholders are rank-and-file employees (82%) and senior management (79%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report who or what is driving the behavior and provide quantified breakdowns of influential groups. This helps journalists understand motives and audiences. Avoid unsupported causal claims—use survey data or evidence to substantiate attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology: The Council distributed the survey to more than 1,000 private and publicly traded companies across a wide variety of industries in July 2021... A total of 82 companies provided usable responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a succinct methodology section that states timeframe, distribution method, sampling frame, sample size, and any data-cleaning or validation steps. Transparency about methods allows reporters to assess reliability. Avoid burying sample size or methods; report them prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational boilerplate ('About' section)
rubrics_metrics.description: About the Foundation for Public Affairs... About the Public Affairs Council... Both nonpartisan and nonpolitical, the Public Affairs Council is the leading association for public affairs professionals worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with short boilerplate paragraphs that explain the releasing organizations, mission, and a URL. Boilerplates should be factual and standardized so journalists and editors can reuse them. Avoid marketing copy that reads like an advertisement—keep it informational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to action and links to full materials / resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Visit our website to view the full reports here. More News & Resources. Spring Executive Conference... Learn More
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit calls to action and direct links to the full report, related resources, and upcoming events. Make links and directions prominent so readers can access source documents. Avoid leaving readers without a clear next step or link to primary materials.
